title: Dark Energy Might Not Be Constant After All, New Supernova Study Suggests
summary:
Dark energy is the mysterious force that's making the universe expand faster and faster. For decades, scientists assumed it was constant — unchanging, like a cosmic setting stuck on one number. But a new study of nearly 3,000 exploding stars suggests that assumption might be wrong.

The study focused on type Ia supernovas. These happen when a white dwarf — the leftover core of a dead star — pulls material from a companion star until it explodes. Because these explosions are almost always the same brightness, scientists call them "standard candles." They use them like cosmic measuring tapes to figure out how far away things are.

The team rebuilt three decades of astronomical observations into one consistent framework. They combined their supernova data with other measurements, including relic light from the Big Bang and maps of how galaxies are spread through space.

"Instead of confirming the standard model of cosmology, which assumes dark energy is fixed and unchanging, we have more evidence that dark energy may change over time," said Ryan Camilleri of the University of Queensland.

This isn't the first hint. In 2024, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) found similar clues. Now, two independent measurements point in the same direction: dark energy might be time-varying.

"Two completely independent measurements have found hints of time variation in dark energy, challenging the standard model," said Davis, a team member.

If dark energy really does change, it could reshape our understanding of the universe. It might even help explain how gravity and quantum physics fit together — two theories that scientists have never been able to unite.

The team's catalog will grow with new data from the DEBASS program, which is detecting hundreds more local supernovas. More data means a clearer picture of what dark energy actually is.
why_it_matters: Dark energy is thought to make up most of the universe, so if it turns out to change over time, the basic physics students learn about how the cosmos works may have to be rewritten.

background_read: In the late 1990s, two competing teams of astronomers studied distant supernovas to measure how fast the universe was expanding. They expected gravity to be slowing the expansion down; instead, they found it was speeding up.

That surprise gave birth to the idea of dark energy — an unknown something that seems to make up most of the universe's energy. The discovery later earned a Nobel Prize in Physics for Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess.

Astronomers call their standard picture of the universe the "standard model of cosmology" (also known as Lambda-CDM). It assumes dark energy is a constant — the same number everywhere, at every time — and that is exactly the assumption this new study tests.

The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), mentioned in the article, is a real instrument on a telescope in Arizona that maps millions of galaxies to trace how the universe has stretched over time.
Type Ia supernovas are rare and hard to catch, so astronomers keep building bigger catalogues. The DEBASS program is the latest effort to add hundreds more nearby examples.

perspectives.description: A catalogue built from three decades of data gives the strongest hint yet that dark energy varies. Two independent measurements agreeing is exactly the kind of confirmation scientists look for, and it opens the door to a deeper theory of the universe.

The article calls these findings 'hints', not proof. Supernova measurements are notoriously sensitive to tiny errors, and the standard model of cosmology has survived many earlier challenges. Until the data set grows, some astronomers will argue that a constant dark energy is still the safest explanation.

Cosmology has been overturned before: in the late 1990s, astronomers expecting the expansion to slow down found it speeding up instead. Science often advances when two independent lines of evidence start disagreeing with a long-accepted model.

New surveys such as DESI, DEBASS and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile — designed to photograph the whole southern sky again and again — will add far more supernovas. More data will either sharpen the hint of time-varying dark energy or make it fade away.
